A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MTSQL-R1. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including material relocated between versions.

before.justification: v2 reports original CoSQL/SParC experiments, training-stage and tool ablations, error analyses, training dynamics, and case studies.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, transfer evaluations, predicted-history testing, reward ablations, and inference-budget experiments.

M1.justification: Section 3.3.2 changes the stated reward aggregation from four separately weighted terms to two groups: EX plus EM, and all process rewards. The action loop, self-taught SFT algorithm, and GRPO procedure remain intact. This establishes a limited objective revision, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluation on Spider and BIRD using a CoSQL-trained model, plus a CoSQL scenario conditioned on model-generated prior SQL (Tables 6 and 12). These expand benchmark coverage and input conditions beyond v2. First-turn evaluation within CoSQL/SParC already existed; industrial scenarios discussed in v3 are not evaluated.

E2.justification: v3 Table 2 adds short-horizon Direct RL at 1.7B/4B and a LangGraph planning/tool agent, while dropping the Qwen3-8B rows and untrained long-horizon 14B row from that comparison. Table 12 introduces single-turn comparators including DAIL-SQL+GPT-4, CHASE-SQL+Gemini 1.5, and RESDSQL-3B+NatSQ. These substantially expand the evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: v3 introduces a LLaMA3.2-3B-Instruct setting, gold-versus-predicted-history testing, reward-component controls, and 2,000/4,000/6,000/8,000-token inference caps. Appendix D.6 specifies extracting intermediate SQL when truncation prevents completion. The efficiency comparison changes from v2 Table 8's averaged EX to CoSQL-specific evaluation in v3 Table 13; the original Qwen training configuration largely remains unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds reward-component ablations separating verification from proposal/correction rewards, token-budget sensitivity, and predicted-history robustness tests. Its error chart also adds the SFT-only stage between base and SFT+RL (Figure 6). The earlier tool ablations, turn/difficulty analyses, training dynamics, and case studies are retained, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: v3 Table 10 introduces ± reporting for reward-ablation results, including 79.1±0.15 EX for the previously reported outcome-only result of 79.1. Neither the meaning of these quantities nor run counts or seeds is specified, so additional runs and statistical significance cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include predicted-history CoSQL EX of 76.5 versus Direct RL's 71.2, Spider/BIRD EX of 84.2/56.9, and architectural-transfer, reward-ablation, and token-budget outcomes. Most original Table 2 cells remain, but the full 4B model's out-of-domain CoSQL EM changes from 62.9 to 63.0, alongside edited averages. The replacement efficiency results use different settings and do not establish same-setting improvements.

T1.justification: The total-reward definition in Section 3.3.2 now imposes shared coefficients within outcome and process groups, replacing four coefficients with two. This changes the formal weighting specification. The MDP definitions, transition structure, and SFT/GRPO expressions otherwise remain substantively unchanged; Algorithm 1 is relocated rather than newly introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: an MDP-based long-horizon SQL agent, execution/memory verification, self-taught SFT followed by RL, and superior CoSQL/SParC performance. Reworded contribution bullets and additional supporting experiments do not materially redefine these headline claims.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands interpretation of deployment robustness, efficiency trade-offs, truncation failures, and real-time applicability. Section 5 and Appendix C.3 discuss industrial schema retrieval, alternative memory backends, and compatibility with large-model distillation pipelines as untested extensions. v2 already acknowledged higher token costs, but lacked these detailed applicability arguments and qualifications.

D1.justification: v3 newly identifies basic vLLM as the latency-measurement implementation and describes absent inference optimizations. A configuration comment clarifies that KL loss was already disabled. The release promise changes from after internal review to upon acceptance, with the explicit artifact list removed. Hardware, learning rates, tool templates, and most configuration details are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting DAIL-SQL, RESDSQL, CHASE-SQL, LLaMA, and production-agent latency discussion. Section 4.4 also changes attribution of the error taxonomy from prior work to the authors' design. The main related-work positioning remains stable; merged duplicate SQL-R1 references and publication updates do not represent different cited works.

P1.justification: RQ1 is substantially reordered into grouped effectiveness, generalization/robustness, and efficiency arguments. Training dynamics moves from Section 4.5 to Appendix D.8, Algorithm 1 moves to Appendix A, and a Discussion section is introduced. The appendix organization is extensively revised, alongside terminology standardization and prose tightening.

P2.justification: Table 2 is reorganized by backbone and reasoning horizon, removes its combined Average column, and adds comparison rows. v3 introduces several evaluation tables and two Pareto plots, and redraws the error chart with an SFT-only series. Original figures are extensively redistributed between main text and appendices, with difficulty accuracy also displayed separately.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important gaps in v2's empirical support through trained Direct RL controls, component-level reward ablations, and testing with model-generated dialogue histories. Transfer and token-budget experiments further strengthen assessment of generality and practical costs. These substantially improve the evidence for the framework despite narrower latency-comparator coverage, unexplained ± quantities, and limited implementation detail for some new baselines.
